title: Properties of the Transform
intro: A handful of rules say what each operation on a signal does to its transform: shifting, scaling, modulating, multiplying, convolving and differentiating. They turn a table of a dozen pairs into a table of thousands, and they explain why a signal cannot be short in both time and frequency.

blocks.text: Why rules

Write $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(f)$ to say that $X$ is the transform of $x$. The table on the From Series to Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/series-to-transform) page holds a few pairs. The rules here let you build the rest from them without integrating again. Each rule follows from one line of the defining integral, and the geometric content of each is easy to picture, as arrows turning and stretching.
Linearity

$a\,x(t) + b\,y(t) \leftrightarrow a\,X(f) + b\,Y(f)$. The integral is linear. This is why a sum of sinusoids has a spectrum that is the sum of their spectra, and it is the property all the others lean on.
Time shift

$x(t - t_0) \leftrightarrow e^{-j2\pi f t_0}X(f)$. Substituting $t' = t - t_0$ in the integral pulls out the factor $e^{-j2\pi f t_0}$. Its magnitude is 1: shifting never changes how much of each frequency there is, only where each starts. Its angle is $-360^\circ f t_0$, a straight line in $f$. A delay of $t_0 = 0.25$ s turns the phase at $f = 1, 2, 3$ Hz by $-90^\circ,\ -180^\circ,\ -270^\circ$. The Reading a Spectrum (#/math/fourier-transform/spectrum) page showed this as linear phase.
Frequency shift and modulation
$e^{j2\pi f_0 t}x(t) \leftrightarrow X(f - f_0)$: multiplying by a turning arrow slides the whole spectrum along the frequency axis. In practice the multiplier is a cosine, which is two arrows:

blocks.tex: x(t)\cos(2\pi f_0 t) \leftrightarrow \tfrac12\left[X(f - f_0) + X(f + f_0)\right]

blocks.text: This is how a radio works. Take the 0.5 s pulse with $X(0) = 0.5$ and multiply it by a 100 Hz cosine. The spectrum becomes two humps of half the height, $0.25$, centred at $\pm100$ Hz, each with the sinc shape, with its first zeros at $100 \pm 2$ Hz, that is 98 and 102 Hz. The message has been moved to a frequency where it can be sent.

The shift rule and the time-shift rule are mirror images, and the same rule holds for the Laplace transform, where $e^{-at}$ shifts the surface in the $\sigma$ direction. Try it below. The damped cosine $e^{-at}\cos(\omega_0 t)u(t)$ is the decaying exponential times a cosine, so its transform is half the exponential's $1/(a + j\omega)$ shifted to $+\omega_0$ and half to $-\omega_0$.

With a = 0.5 and ω₀ = 1.5, the slice panel, which plots $|X(j\omega)|$ along the axis, peaks near ω = 1.5, where the readout says $|X| = 1.040$. It is the sum of two complex numbers: the exponential shifted to $+\omega_0$ contributes $\tfrac12\cdot 1/a = 1.0$, and its mirror image at $-\omega_0$ contributes $0.027 - 0.162j$ (size 0.164). Move Frequency ω₀ to 2.0 and the peak slides to ω = 2 with nearly the same height; the unshifted exponential (signal: decaying exponential) peaks at 0 with height $1/a = 2$.
Scaling

$x(at) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{|a|}X(f/a)$. Speed the signal up by a factor $a$ and its spectrum spreads by the same factor and drops by $1/a$. A 0.5 s pulse has its first spectral zero at 2 Hz; a 0.25 s pulse has it at 4 Hz, and a 1 s pulse at 1 Hz. Compressing in time stretches in frequency, exactly the reciprocal relation seen in the rectangle.
Duality

The formulas for $X(f)$ and $x(t)$ differ only by the sign in the exponent. So if $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(f)$, then $X(t) \leftrightarrow x(-f)$. The rectangle and the sinc are the clearest case: $\operatorname{rect}(t) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{sinc}(f)$, hence $\operatorname{sinc}(t) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{rect}(f)$. A sinc in time is exactly a flat band in frequency, the ideal low-pass filter's impulse response.
Convolution and multiplication
The convolution of two signals is $(x * h)(t) = \int x(\tau)h(t - \tau)\,d\tau$, the output of a linear filter with impulse response $h$ driven by $x$. Its transform is a product:

blocks.tex: x * h \leftrightarrow X(f)\,H(f), \qquad x\cdot h \leftrightarrow X * H

blocks.text: Convolution in one domain is multiplication in the other. This is the reason frequency response works: to filter a signal, multiply its spectrum by $H(f)$ frequency by frequency. A worked case: convolve a 1 s rectangle with itself. The result is a triangle of height 1 and base 2. By the rule its transform is $\operatorname{sinc}(f)^2$, for example $\operatorname{sinc}(0.5)^2 = 0.6366^2 = 0.4053$. Squaring pushes the sinc's side lobes down, which is why triangles are smoother than rectangles and have a faster-falling spectrum, as the Convergence and the Gibbs Phenomenon (#/math/fourier-transform/convergence) page predicted.
Differentiation

$x'(t) \leftrightarrow j2\pi f\, X(f)$. Differentiating $e^{j2\pi f t}$ multiplies it by $j2\pi f$, and by linearity this applies to every component. The magnitude is multiplied by $2\pi f$: high frequencies are amplified and low ones suppressed. Differentiating $\cos(2\pi\cdot 3t)$ gives a wave of amplitude $2\pi\cdot3 = 18.85$. This is why differentiation amplifies noise, and why a signal with a jump has a spectrum falling only like $1/f$: its derivative has an impulse, whose spectrum is flat, and dividing by $j2\pi f$ gives $1/f$.
Energy

Parseval for the transform: $\int|x(t)|^2dt = \int|X(f)|^2df$. For $e^{-t}u(t)$, the energy in time is $\int_0^\infty e^{-2t}dt = \tfrac12$. In frequency, $\int\frac{df}{1 + 4\pi^2f^2} = \tfrac12$ as well. The same energy counted two ways.
Uncertainty: short in time, narrow in frequency

The scaling rule has a consequence. Shrink a pulse to half its width and its spectrum doubles in width. No scaling trick can make both narrow. Define the width of a signal as the RMS spread of its energy, $\sigma_t^2 = \int t^2|x|^2dt\big/\int|x|^2dt$, and likewise $\sigma_f$ for $|X|^2$. Then

The Gaussian $e^{-\pi t^2}$ reaches the equality. Here $|x|^2 = e^{-2\pi t^2}$, a Gaussian of variance $\sigma_t^2 = 1/(4\pi)$, so $\sigma_t = 0.2821$, and since $X(f) = e^{-\pi f^2}$ has the same form, $\sigma_f = 0.2821$ too. The product is $0.2821^2 = 0.0796 = 1/(4\pi)$. Stretch the Gaussian by $s$, $e^{-\pi(t/s)^2}$, and $\sigma_t = s/(2\sqrt\pi)$ grows while $\sigma_f = 1/(2\sqrt\pi\, s)$ shrinks:

The product is $0.0796$ every time. No signal does better, and the Gaussian is the one that does not waste any. For a rectangle the bound is far from reached: its width $\tau$ and first null $1/\tau$ have a product of 1. This is the same inequality as Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics: a particle's position and momentum wavefunctions are a Fourier pair. It is a fact about waves, not about measurement.

widget.title: A delay moves phase, not amplitude

blocks.text: From the side, the bars show the amplitudes 0.811, 0.090, 0.032, 0.017 at 1, 3, 5, 7 Hz. Move Delay from 0 to 0.25 and then 0.5: the bars never change, while the phase panel's points turn by $-90^\circ k$ and $-180^\circ k$ for harmonic $k$. At Delay = 0.5 every odd harmonic flips sign (phase 180°) and the triangle is turned upside down. That is the time-shift rule acting on a periodic signal.
Practice

blocks.title: Shift the phase
blocks.text: A signal is delayed by 0.25 s. What happens to its transform at 2 Hz?
solution: The factor is $e^{-j2\pi\cdot 2\cdot 0.25} = e^{-j\pi} = -1$. The magnitude is unchanged and the phase moves by $-180^\circ$: the 2 Hz component is inverted. At 1 Hz it would be $-90^\circ$, at 3 Hz $-270^\circ$.

blocks.title: Stretch a Gaussian
blocks.text: Find the transform of $e^{-\pi(t/2)^2}$ and its RMS width in frequency.
solution: Scaling with $a = 1/2$: $x(at)$ with $x = e^{-\pi t^2}$ gives $\frac{1}{|a|}X(f/a) = 2e^{-\pi(2f)^2} = 2e^{-4\pi f^2}$. Stretched twofold in time, the transform is twice as tall and half as wide. $\sigma_f = 1/(2\sqrt\pi\cdot 2) = 0.1410$, and $\sigma_t\sigma_f = 0.5642\times 0.1410 = 0.0796$, the Gaussian minimum.

blocks.title: Modulate a pulse
blocks.text: Multiply the 0.5 s pulse by $\cos(2\pi\cdot 100 t)$. Where is its spectrum, and how tall is it?
solution: The pulse has $X(f) = 0.5\operatorname{sinc}(0.5f)$. The product has $\tfrac12[X(f - 100) + X(f + 100)]$: two copies centred at $\pm 100$ Hz, each of height $\tfrac12\times 0.5 = 0.25$, with first zeros 2 Hz either side, at 98 and 102 Hz (and the mirror pair at $-98$, $-102$).

blocks.title: Differentiate a cosine
blocks.text: What is the amplitude of the derivative of $\cos(2\pi\cdot 3t)$, and what does that say about noise?
solution: The derivative is $-2\pi\cdot3\sin(2\pi\cdot3t)$, amplitude $18.85$. The gain is $2\pi f$, so it grows with frequency: at 300 Hz the gain is 100 times what it is at 3 Hz. Any high-frequency noise riding on a signal is boosted far more than the signal itself, so differentiation makes a measurement noisier.
blocks.answer: $18.85$; the gain $2\pi f$ amplifies high-frequency noise.
